Q: STM32 Modbus TCP A:

https://github.com/cesanta/mongoose/ provides both embedded web server and modbus-tcp server.

Here is the web dashboard with modbus-tcp example: https://github.com/cesanta/mongoose/tree/master/tutorials/tcp/modbus-dashboard

Mongoose can run on top of LWIP or be stand-alone, since it has its own TCP/IP stack with drivers (STM32 Ethernet included)

Q: How Should a Table Reference Two Columns That Have a Many-to-Many Relationship? A:

Presuming your Brands and Suppliers tables are defined as such:

CREATE TABLE Brands (
    ID   INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
    Name NVARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE Suppliers (
    ID   INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
    Name NVARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

Your bridge table BrandsSuppliers should be constructed this way:

CREATE TABLE BrandsSuppliers (
    BrandID    INT NOT NULL,
    SupplierID INT NOT NULL,

    PRIMARY KEY (BrandID, SupplierID),

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandID)    REFERENCES Brands(ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (SupplierID) REFERENCES Suppliers(ID)
);

We use composite primary key (BrandID, SupplierID) with each component referencing to 2 other table's PKs, that is the simplest way to ensure itself's uniqueness, and it also ensure as long as a row (or pair) in this table exists, the relative brand and supplier must exist. We can of course create its own primary key ID but since this table totally depends on the other two, there's no point to add another new column for such purpose. Also, using a separate stand-alone PK would requires us to add another constraint to ensure the row's uniqueness. (explained below)

And this is how your Products table can directly reference the bridge table (AKA junction table):

CREATE TABLE Products (
    ID         INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
    Name       NVARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    BrandID    INT           NOT NULL,
    SupplierID INT           NOT NULL,

    CONSTRAINT FK_Product_BrandSupplier
        FOREIGN KEY (BrandID, SupplierID) REFERENCES BrandsSuppliers(BrandID, SupplierID)
);

It's quite straightforward. However, there are times when we need to write queries which need to JOIN between Products and Brands tables, or bwteen Products and Suppliers table. Without direct FK/PK relationship between the two tables, it's still valid to use JOIN clause but it would not leverage the relationship directly. So it would be a better idea to add the FK/PK relationship between Products and Brands, as well as between Products and Suppliers, like so:

CREATE TABLE Products (
    ID         INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
    Name       NVARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    BrandID    INT           NOT NULL,
    SupplierID INT           NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandID)    REFERENCES Brands(ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (SupplierID) REFERENCES Suppliers(ID),
    CONSTRAINT FK_Product_BrandSupplier
        FOREIGN KEY (BrandID, SupplierID) REFERENCES BrandsSuppliers(BrandID, SupplierID)
);

Adding the 2 FK references also makes relationship clearer for those who read the schema.

What if BrandsSuppliers has its own PK column

It can have its own primary key, maybe like this way:

CREATE TABLE BrandsSuppliers (
    ID         INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
    BrandID    INT NOT NULL,
    SupplierID INT NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandID)    REFERENCES Brands(ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (SupplierID) REFERENCES Suppliers(ID),

    CONSTRAINT UQ_BrandSupplier UNIQUE (BrandID, SupplierID)  -- needed by many-to-many relationship
);

We need to add that UNIQUE constraint to ensure the row (relationship) is unqiue because many-to-many relationship demands that.

And now we might be tempted to change the design of Products table like so:

-- NOTE: this is a bad idea
CREATE TABLE Products (
    ID              INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
    Name            NVARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    BrandID         INT NOT NULL,
    SupplierID      INT NOT NULL,
    BrandSupplierID INT NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandID)         REFERENCES Brands(ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (SupplierID)      REFERENCES Suppliers(ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (BrandSupplierID) REFERENCES BrandsSuppliers(ID)
);

However, this would bring a new problem. It is highly possible that the certain product could reference to a book not in the brand-supplier relationship, or the supplier is missing in the relationship. This is problematic. We are thus forced to remove those 2 FK/PK relationship and consequently the 2 columns as well, like so:

-- Better, but not good enough.
CREATE TABLE Products (
    ID              INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
    Name            NVARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    BrandSupplierID INT NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandSupplierID) REFERENCES BrandsSuppliers(ID)
);

That means if we wan to look up a product's brand info or the supplier info, we must route through the BrandsSuppliers table first. It would be 2 JOIN clauses instead of just 1. So, using composite primary key in BrandsSuppliers table is a better solution.

Q: Xcode Preview crash with ModelContainer initialization A:

I eventually discovered that the issue was not caused by the code in my original question.

The actual problem was that one of my SwiftData models was named Transaction, which conflicts with Swift's Transactiontype from StoreKit.

Because of this naming conflict, Xcode Preview was crashing with the strange ModelContainer initialization error.

After renaming my SwiftData model from Transaction to something else, everything started working normally.

One useful clue is that if there is a naming conflict, the syntax highlighting color of that model name in the Xcode editor may look different from your other SwiftData models.

So if you're seeing a similar issue, check whether any of your SwiftData model names conflict with types defined by Apple frameworks.

Reference: Apple — StoreKit Transaction

Q: Configure VS Code `Enter` as newline, not send Copilot Chat prompt A:

Use the Keyboard Shortcuts menu item Open Keyboard Shortcuts (JSON) and delete the default Enter submit binding; then add Enter binding to the type command with "\n". This will cause Enter to add a new line, and Ctrl+Enter to send the prompt.

Q: curl: (35) SSL connect error, NSS error -5938 A:

It is a mismatch between your curl / openssl version (and libraries between) that do not accept 2018 best cipher, and this particular server that only support those cipher.

Other domain may or may not support more cipher and so curl may (or not) be able to query them.

Only way to fix that: update (or possibly upgrade up to 6.10).

In the future, this can happen again if security increase again.
